name: Ben Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my Uncle Keith's building firm, there's four of us, and we do extensions, loft conversions and roof repairs round the town and the villages. Today I was up on a roof in Church Lane replacing rotten rafters, tomorrow it's a kitchen extension out on the Mill Road. I'm the junior, so I'm on the mixer, the barrow and the ladder a lot, and Keith's teaching me the carpentry bit by bit. I'm slower than I should be at twenty-seven, I won't pretend otherwise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people know us. Mrs Hollis gives us tea and biscuits every morning, and her son was in my class at school. What wears me out is the weather and the paperwork Keith brings home, he's always complaining about the forms. I didn't finish school, I was always better with my hands, and this is the first thing I've done that I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, that it's mostly people in cities getting excited about computers. Round here people want a man they know to fix their roof. I'd say it at the pub and after church, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, and I'm glad. I get to learn the trade from Keith properly, the way he learned it from my grandad. Maybe one day I take over the firm when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, keep working, keep putting a bit by. I've got about three months saved, and I'm putting the rest towards a ring for Hannah, my girlfriend, she's a hairdresser in town. I'd like to propose next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. It's how I'd want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I've got a phone for calls and the football scores, that's it. Keith's daughter set him up with something for his quotes, and he swore at it for a week and went back to his notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned taking over the firm one day. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keith's said it a couple of times, after a pint. He's got no sons in the trade, and my dad passed when I was nineteen, so Keith's sort of looked out for me. I'd want to earn it first, though, not be handed it.

S0.say: I'd say at the pub and after church that it was mostly city people getting excited about computers. Round here people want someone they know to fix their roof.
S0.think: Privately he's glad nothing changes, because he can learn the trade from his uncle the way his uncle learned it. One day he might take over the firm.
S0.do: Keeps working at his uncle's firm and keeps about three months saved. Puts the rest towards an engagement ring for his girlfriend Hannah, planning to propose next spring.
S0.feel: Calm and content, the way he'd want it.
S0.quote: Keith's daughter set him up with something for his quotes, and he swore at it for a week and went back to his notebook.
S0.fieldNote: Ben's world is a small family firm in a market town where customers know the builders by name. He's never used AI and sees it as a city thing. Family runs through everything: his late father, his uncle as mentor and a proposal planned for spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but a computer's not coming to fix Mrs Hollis's guttering. Maybe the big firms change, but the little ones like us will be fine. I'd say people should work for what they've got and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd mostly be all right. Our work's old houses, wonky walls, every job different. The bit that worries me is Keith's paperwork, if the council and the suppliers all go onto AI systems, he'd struggle and so would I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, same as now. Maybe Keith's daughter would have to do the forms for us, she's good with that stuff. I wouldn't go learning computers unless I really had to, I'd wait and see what the other small builders round here do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a niggle about the forms, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said little firms will be fine. What if a big firm with machines started undercutting you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd lose some jobs, I suppose. But people round here are loyal, they'd pay a bit more for someone they trust. My grandad said the same when the big DIY shops came, and we're still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the lads I was at school with who work on the big estates outside town. That's the same house over and over, and I can see a machine doing that. I'd tell them to come and find small work like ours.

S1.say: I'd say a computer isn't coming to fix Mrs Hollis's guttering, and small firms like ours will be fine. People should work for what they've got and get on with it.
S1.think: Privately he thinks they'd mostly be fine because they work on irregular old houses. What worries him is paperwork going onto AI systems, which he and his uncle would struggle with.
S1.do: Keeps working as he does now and hopes his uncle's daughter would handle any new digital forms. Waits to see what other small builders in the area do before learning any computer tools.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a niggle about the paperwork.
S1.quote: My grandad said the same when the big DIY shops came, and we're still here.
S1.fieldNote: Ben trusts local loyalty and family history to protect small firms. His one real worry is paperwork going digital, not robots on roofs. He would rely on family, a cousin, to handle the tech side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, letting a few tech companies turn everything upside down that fast. I'd say people should look after their own, families and churches, because you can't wait for the government. I don't post online much, but I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. If a robot can go up a ladder and replace a rafter, and it's cheaper than us, even Mrs Hollis would have to think about it. I've got no school certificates and no other trade, so I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd save every penny I could and stop going out so much. I'd still propose to Hannah, I'm not putting that off because of a computer, but we'd have a small wedding at the church hall. Once it arrives, I'd lean on family, Keith, my mum, Hannah's lot, and do any odd jobs people still want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's moving and I can't get my footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't put off the proposal. Why does that matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how you get through hard times, you've got your people. My mum and dad got married in a bad year, Dad was laid off from the quarry that same month, and they managed. I'd rather face it with Hannah than on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, would you try to learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I wouldn't know where to start. I'm not going to be fixing robots, I can barely work the satnav. Maybe I'd ask at church, there are older men there who've been through a factory closing, they'd have more sense than me.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong for a few tech companies to turn everything upside down so fast. People should look after their own, families and churches, rather than wait for government.
S2.think: Privately he'd be scared: if a robot can replace a rafter cheaper, even loyal customers would think about it. With no certificates or other trade, he doesn't know what he'd do.
S2.do: Saves every penny and goes out less in the two years before. Still proposes to Hannah but plans a small church-hall wedding, then leans on family and does odd jobs people still want a person for.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground moving under his feet.
S2.quote: I'd still propose to Hannah, I'm not putting that off because of a computer, but we'd have a small wedding at the church hall.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks his confidence in local loyalty. He blames tech companies rather than markets in general, and turns to family and church rather than the state. Refusing to delay the proposal was his firmest statement, rooted in his parents' story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more decent, people can get ready. I'd say firms should take on apprentices and keep them on, not just bring in machines. That's what I believe in, learning a trade from someone who knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still scares me, just slower. I'd be thirty-two and maybe just about a proper carpenter, and then it doesn't matter. At least I'd have a few years to get married and settle a bit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Keith and get as good as I can, fast. I'd save more, try to get to six months. Maybe I'd start doing the quoting and talking to customers with Keith, because if anything lasts, it's people wanting someone they trust to sort the job out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the fast one, but it's there every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should keep apprentices on. Would you expect government to make them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't want the government forcing it, no. But I'd hope the decent firms would do it because it's right. Keith took me on when nobody else would, that's how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about how you work, with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe let Keith's daughter show me the computer quoting thing. I'd hate it, but I'd do it if it meant keeping the firm going. I'd draw the line at talking to a robot, mind.

S3.say: I'd say five years is more decent and people can get ready. Firms should take on apprentices and keep them, not just bring in machines.
S3.think: Privately it still scares him, only slower: at thirty-two he'd just be a proper carpenter when it stops mattering. At least he could marry and settle first.
S3.do: Keeps working for his uncle and tries to improve quickly while building savings towards six months. Starts helping with quoting and customer contact, and reluctantly learns the computer quoting tool to keep the firm going.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, though less than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd hate it, but I'd do it if it meant keeping the firm going. I'd draw the line at talking to a robot, mind.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts Ben towards the customer-facing side of the firm, betting on trust lasting. He wants firms to keep apprentices out of decency, not by law. Loyalty to his uncle is what would push him to touch technology at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to sort themselves out, if they're willing to work. I'd say families should plan for it, like you plan for anything. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far off. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with a kid, maybe running the firm with Keith. Then the robots turn up and I don't know what happens, but that's a long way away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing different. I'd propose to Hannah in the spring like I planned, keep working and keep saving. Maybe in a few years, if I saw it coming, I'd talk to Keith about what the firm should do, but I'd leave that to him really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly I'd try not to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave it to Keith. What if Keith retires before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I suppose it's on me, and that's a frightening thought. I'd have to learn the business side whether I liked it or not. I'd want to have Hannah with me on that, she's better with money than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children with ten years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. You can't stop living because of what might happen in ten years. My grandparents had five kids with less than we've got.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people willing to work to sort themselves out, and families should plan for it. I wouldn't make a fuss.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels far off; he'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe running the firm with his uncle. What happens after that is a long way away.
S4.do: Proposes to Hannah in the spring as planned, keeps working and saving, and leaves the firm's strategy mostly to his uncle. Expects to learn the business side if his uncle retires first.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly trying not to think about it.
S4.quote: You can't stop living because of what might happen in ten years.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ben goes back to his life plan almost unchanged: proposal, marriage, maybe children. He defers strategy to his uncle until asked what happens if Keith retires first, which visibly unsettled him. His grandparents serve as his model for getting by on less.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no trade to fall back on and no time to find one. What would help is the small firms getting a fair chance, and decent firms keeping their apprentices on. And family and church pulling together, that's what's always got people through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old buildings. Half the houses in our town are two hundred years old, and you learn them by getting it wrong. I'd want somebody left who knows how they were built.

headlineQuote: Half the houses in our town are two hundred years old, and you learn them by getting it wrong.
portrait: Ben Abbott is a 27-year-old junior in his Uncle Keith's four-person building firm in a market town, doing roofs, lofts and extensions for customers who know him by name. He has about three months saved, has never used AI, and is saving for a ring for his girlfriend Hannah. He is calm if AI fizzles or change is steady, trusting local loyalty, but alarmed by AGI in two years because he has no other trade. Whatever happens he refuses to put off the proposal, and he looks to family and church more than government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have no trade to fall back on and no time to find one.
whatWouldHelp: A fair chance for small firms, decent firms keeping their apprentices, and family and church pulling together.
